title: Advanced Python: comprehensions, generators, decorators
summary: Write concise comprehensions, memory-efficient generators, and reusable decorators to make your Python cleaner, faster, and more Pythonic.
objectives: Build lists, dicts and sets with comprehensions
Add filtering conditions inside a comprehension
Explain why generators save memory with large data
Understand that functions are first-class objects
Write and apply a basic decorator with @
Choose the right tool: comprehension, generator, or loop

quiz.q: What does the comprehension [x*x for x in range(4)] produce?
quiz.why: range(4) gives 0,1,2,3, and squaring each gives 0, 1, 4, 9.

quiz.q: Which keyword turns a function into a generator?
quiz.why: yield produces a value and pauses the function, resuming where it left off on the next request.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a generator over building a full list?
quiz.why: A generator yields one item at a time instead of holding every item in memory, so it scales to huge or infinite sequences.

quiz.q: In Python, what does it mean that functions are first-class objects?
quiz.answer: Functions can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions, just like any other value.
quiz.why: This is exactly what makes decorators possible — a decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one.

quiz.q: What does the @ symbol do above a function definition?
quiz.answer: It applies a decorator — it wraps the function below it with the named decorator function.
quiz.why: @timer above def work() is shorthand for work = timer(work).

quiz.q: Rewrite this loop as a list comprehension: result = []; for n in nums: if n > 0: result.append(n)
quiz.answer: [n for n in nums if n > 0]
quiz.why: The expression comes first, then the for clause, then the optional if filter.

body_markdown:
## Comprehensions: build collections in one line

A **comprehension** is a compact way to build a list, dictionary, or set from an existing iterable. Instead of creating an empty list and appending in a loop, you describe the whole result in one expression.

```python
# the long way
squares = []
for x in range(5):
    squares.append(x * x)

# the comprehension
squares = [x * x for x in range(5)]   # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
```

You can add an `if` to filter, and the same pattern works for dicts and sets.

```python
evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]   # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in ["hi", "world"]}  # {'hi': 2, 'world': 5}
unique = {c for c in "banana"}                  # {'b', 'a', 'n'}
```

## Generators: one item at a time

A comprehension builds the whole collection in memory. A **generator** produces values lazily — one at a time, only when asked. You write one with a function that uses `yield` instead of `return`.

```python
def count_up_to(limit):
    n = 1
    while n <= limit:
        yield n
        n += 1

for value in count_up_to(3):
    print(value)   # 1, then 2, then 3
```

Each call to `yield` hands back a value and **pauses** the function; it resumes from that exact spot next time. This means a generator can describe a sequence too big to fit in memory — even an infinite one.

## Why generators save memory

If you build a list of ten million squares, all ten million live in memory at once. A generator holds only the current value and a little state, so memory stays flat no matter how long the sequence is. Use a **generator expression** — just round brackets instead of square — when you only iterate once.

```python
total = sum(x * x for x in range(10_000_000))   # tiny memory footprint
```

## Functions are first-class objects

In Python a function is just a value. You can store it in a variable, pass it to another function, or return it from one. This is the foundation decorators are built on.

```python
def shout(text):
    return text.upper()

say = shout          # store the function itself
print(say("hi"))     # HI
```

## Decorators: wrap behaviour around a function

A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a new one with extra behaviour added — logging, timing, access checks — without changing the original code. The `@name` syntax above a definition applies it.

```python
import functools

def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        import time
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def slow_add(a, b):
    return a + b

slow_add(2, 3)   # prints timing, returns 5
```

## Your task

Take a `for` loop from an earlier lesson and rewrite it as a comprehension. Then write one generator function and one simple decorator that prints a message before and after the wrapped function runs.

slides.sub: Month 2 - Data, SQL & Web APIs  |  Lesson 1
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Two, where we move into data, S Q L, and web A P Is. We open with three tools that separate beginners from confident Python programmers: comprehensions, generators, and decorators. By the end of this lesson you'll write cleaner, faster, and more Pythonic code, and you'll understand exactly when to reach for each one.

slides.title: Comprehensions: one line
bullets: Build a list from an iterable in one expression.
Replaces the empty-list-and-append loop.
Shorter and clearer once you know the pattern.
slides.code:
squares = [x * x for x in range(5)]
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
slides.narration: Let's start with comprehensions. A comprehension is a compact way to build a list from something you can loop over. Instead of creating an empty list and appending inside a for loop, you describe the whole result in a single expression. Read it as: x times x, for each x in range five. The result is zero, one, four, nine, sixteen.

slides.title: Filtering with if
bullets: Add an if clause to keep only some items.
The expression comes first, then for, then if.
Same idea works for dicts and sets.
slides.code:
evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in ["hi", "world"]}
slides.narration: You can filter inside a comprehension by adding an if clause at the end. Here we keep only the even numbers. The order is always the same: the expression first, then the for clause, then the optional if. And the very same pattern builds dictionaries and sets — just swap the square brackets for curly braces.

slides.title: Generators: yield
bullets: Produce values one at a time, on demand.
Use yield instead of return.
yield pauses, then resumes where it left off.
slides.narration: Now generators. A comprehension builds the whole collection at once. A generator instead produces values lazily, one at a time, only when asked. You write one with a function that uses yield instead of return. Each yield hands back a value and pauses the function. The next time you ask, it resumes from exactly that spot, remembering its state.

slides.title: Why generators save memory
bullets: A list holds every item at once.
A generator holds only the current value.
Scales to huge — even infinite — sequences.
slides.code: total = sum(x * x for x in range(10_000_000))
slides.narration: Why does this matter? If you build a list of ten million squares, all ten million sit in memory together. A generator holds only the current value plus a little state, so memory stays flat no matter how long the sequence runs. Notice the round brackets here instead of square ones — that's a generator expression, perfect when you only need to loop through the values once.

slides.title: Functions are values
bullets: A function can be stored in a variable.
It can be passed in or returned from functions.
This is what makes decorators possible.
slides.narration: Before decorators, one key idea: in Python a function is just a value, like a number or a string. You can store it in a variable, pass it as an argument, or return it from another function. We say functions are first-class objects. Here we assign shout to a new name, say, and call it through that name. This flexibility is exactly what makes decorators work.

slides.title: Decorators: wrap behaviour
bullets: A function that takes a function, returns a new one.
Adds behaviour without changing the original.
Apply it with @name above the definition.
slides.narration: A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a new version with extra behaviour wrapped around it — things like timing, logging, or access checks — all without touching the original code. You apply one by writing the at symbol and the decorator's name on the line above a definition. Writing at timer above slow add is just shorthand for: slow add equals timer of slow add.

slides.title: A timing decorator
bullets: wrapper runs code before and after the function.
functools.wraps keeps the original name and docs.
*args and **kwargs pass through any arguments.
slides.narration: Here's the shape of a real decorator. The outer function takes the original function. Inside, we define a wrapper that calls the original and can run code before and after it. We use star args and double-star kwargs so the wrapper accepts any arguments and passes them straight through. The functools wraps line is good manners — it keeps the original function's name and documentation intact.

slides.title: Choosing the right tool
bullets: Comprehension: build a small collection you reuse.
Generator: stream large data, save memory.
Decorator: add the same behaviour to many functions.
Plain loop: complex logic that needs to be clear.
slides.narration: So how do you choose? Reach for a comprehension when you're building a small collection you'll use more than once. Reach for a generator when you're streaming large data and want to save memory. Reach for a decorator when you want to add the same behaviour to many functions. And don't be afraid of a plain loop when the logic is complex — clarity always beats cleverness.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Comprehensions build collections in one line.
Generators yield one item at a time, saving memory.
Functions are values you can pass and return.
Decorators wrap behaviour using @.
Task: write a comprehension, a generator, a decorator.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Comprehensions build lists, dicts, and sets in a single readable line. Generators use yield to produce values one at a time, keeping memory flat. Because functions are first-class values, we can wrap them with decorators using the at symbol. Your task before the next lesson: rewrite one loop as a comprehension, write one generator function, and write one simple decorator that prints a message before and after the function runs.
